forces.title: Elevated UK Data Centre Energy Costs Drive Uncertainty
forces.description: Chris Daker from Allianz UK notes that higher data-centre energy costs are creating near-term uncertainty for the UK's computers and telecoms sector. This directly impacts the operational expenditure (opex) of data centres, potentially reducing profitability and influencing investment decisions within the Data Centre Real Estate sub-industry in the UK. Managing these energy costs will be critical for businesses.

forces.title: Sustained UK Investment Underpins Data Centre Growth
forces.description: Public and private investment in AI and digital infrastructure, through initiatives like the Digital and Technologies Sector Plan, AI Growth Zones, and TechFirst, continues to support the UK computers and telecoms sector. This sustained investment acts as a significant upside driver for Data Centre Real Estate, as digital infrastructure and AI adoption directly translate to increased demand for physical data centre facilities, colocation capacity, and power leasing in the UK.

forces.title: AI Workloads Intensify Data Centre Energy Demand
forces.description: Increasingly powerful AI models are accelerating adoption and driving demand for greater computing power, leading to a considerable increase in electricity demand for AI data centers through 2030, with AI workloads accounting for about 70 percent of the increase. This fundamental shift means higher rack densities and impacts power and space leasing models for Data Centre Real Estate globally, including in the UK.

forces.title: Data Centres Adopting 800-volt DC for Efficiency
forces.description: Data centres are moving towards 800-volt DC (800 VDC) systems to address inefficiencies of traditional low-voltage AC architectures at higher rack densities. This shift reduces current requirements, conductor size, copper usage, and electrical footprint. This structural change influences the design and construction of new data centres, offering lower infrastructure costs and higher revenue-generating capacity, thus impacting Data Centre Real Estate development in the UK.
forces.source_title: The shift to 800-volt DC at data centers: Implications for providers

forces.title: New Power Architectures Offer Significant Cost Savings
forces.description: The transition to 800 VDC systems is projected to significantly improve the economics of data centre operations. Early estimates suggest a 15-18% reduction in capital expenditures on non-IT infrastructure and an 8-10% decrease in power-related operating expenditures. These savings present a strong upside driver for investors and operators in Data Centre Real Estate globally, making new developments more attractive in markets like the UK.

forces.title: Transformer Lead Times Hinder Data Centre Deployment
forces.description: Long lead times for conventional transformers, which can stretch to several years in constrained markets, are a significant headwind for data centre construction and expansion. This delay impacts the speed to market for new facilities, affecting developers and operators in the Data Centre Real Estate sector, including those in the UK. This constraint globally strengthens the case for adopting newer technologies like Solid-State Transformers (SSTs) that can accelerate deployment.
forces.source_title: The shift to 800-volt DC at data centers: Implications for providers

forces.title: Power Architecture Shift Reshapes Data Centre Competition
forces.description: The transition to 800 VDC systems is reshaping the competitive landscape for data centre equipment and services. New entrants from renewables and EV charging, along with venture-backed start-ups, are bringing expertise in high-power conversion. This drives tighter integration between power and cooling, and pushes established electrical equipment companies to adapt. For Data Centre Real Estate in the UK, this means a wider array of suppliers for advanced infrastructure, potentially impacting construction costs, technological innovation, and partnerships with operators.
forces.source_title: The shift to 800-volt DC at data centers: Implications for providers

forces.title: 800 VDC Safety & Workforce Skills Pose Deployment Risks
forces.description: The adoption of 800 VDC in data centres introduces new safety challenges, including different shock, fault, and arc flash risks compared to traditional 48-volt systems. This necessitates new protection strategies, operating procedures, and extensive workforce training for electricians, operators, and IT personnel. These safety and skill-gap issues represent a key risk that could slow the pace of transition and deployment of advanced data centres, potentially impacting the development timeline for Data Centre Real Estate in the UK.

viewpoints.title: UK Data Centres Face Energy Cost Uncertainty Despite Digital Investment
viewpoints.description: Chris Daker, Sector Head for Computers & Telecoms at Allianz UK, notes that while the broader UK computers and telecoms sector shows resilience with public and private investment in AI and digital infrastructure (e.g., Digital and Technologies Sector Plan), "higher data-centre energy costs" are creating near-term uncertainty. This specifically points to a cautious outlook for Data Centre Real Estate in the UK, as operational costs from energy remain a key concern, despite underlying demand drivers from digital adoption. Prudent credit assessment is advised due to these persistent external pressures.

demand_drivers.description: Increasingly powerful AI models enable new applications and create more economic value, driving demand for greater computing power and thus electricity consumption in data centers globally, including the UK.

Modern AI-focused data centers are packing computing power more densely into each rack, with electricity needs climbing from <50 kilowatts to 200-600 kilowatts per rack, and potentially 1 megawatt per rack later this decade, driving demand for more robust facilities.

pnl_drivers.description: Native 800 VDC systems could reduce capital expenditures on non-IT infrastructure by approximately 15 to 18 percent, leading to lower upfront costs for data centre construction and upgrades.

Power-related operating expenditures are projected to decrease by about 8 to 10 percent with 800 VDC architectures, primarily due to reduced electrical losses and improved power usage effectiveness (PUE).
SST-based 800 VDC architectures could reduce copper usage by 40 to 50 percent relative to comparable AC systems, lowering material costs and infrastructure footprint for data centre development.

new_opportunities.description: These campuses are well-positioned to capture greater structural benefits from 800 VDC architectures by designing a high-voltage DC backbone from the outset, optimizing infrastructure costs and efficiency, creating new development opportunities.

market_sizing.methodology: AI workloads are expected to account for about 70 percent of the increase in electricity demand for AI data centers through 2030. Rack power densities are climbing from less than 50 kilowatts per rack to 200 to 600 kilowatts per rack, with projections reaching about one megawatt per rack later this decade. This indicates significant growth in power and space requirements.
